Women's Golf Accessories That Finish the Outfit — and the Round

Every golfer knows the feeling: the outfit is sorted, the tee time is booked, and then you reach into your bag and realise your glove is worn through, your visor is faded, or you are out of tees. Accessories are the quiet half of a golf wardrobe. They are small, they are easy to forget, and they make an outsized difference to how comfortable you are over four or five hours on the course. This is where we keep all of them in one place — the visors, caps, gloves, head covers, tees, ball markers, towels, belt bags and cart accessories that make a round easier and a little more fun.

Sun protection you will actually wear

Golf is one of the few sports where you are outdoors, uncovered, for hours at a stretch. A visor or cap is the single most practical accessory in your bag, and the reason we carry so many of them is that the right one disappears on your head. A slide-on visor keeps your hairstyle intact and lets heat escape through the crown, which is why so many women prefer it in high summer. A full cap gives you coverage across the scalp and is the better choice for pale skin, thinning hair, or a course with very little tree cover. Wide-brim straw styles such as the Daily Sports Dubbo do the most work of all, shading your neck and ears as well as your face.

Alongside headwear, we stock UV-protective sleeves and shoulder wraps. These are worth knowing about if you have ever put on sunscreen at the first tee and then sweated it off by the fifth. A lightweight cooling sleeve stays put, does not need reapplying, and often feels cooler than bare skin because the fabric moves moisture away as it evaporates. If you play in a hot climate or you are careful about sun exposure, this is the accessory category to look at first.

Gloves, and why fit matters more than brand

A golf glove has one job: to keep the club from slipping through your hands without forcing you to grip more tightly than you should. The most common mistake is buying a glove that is slightly too large, because a loose glove bunches at the palm and you end up squeezing the handle to compensate — which tightens the forearms and costs you clubhead speed. A well-fitted glove should feel snug across the palm with no loose fabric, and the fingertips should sit flush with the ends of your fingers.

Consider having two in rotation. Gloves wear out faster when they never get a chance to dry, so alternating between a pair extends the life of both, especially in humid weather. Store them flat rather than crumpled in a pocket, and if a glove gets soaked, let it air-dry away from direct heat so the leather does not stiffen.

Head covers with personality

Head covers protect the crown and face of your woods from the knocks and scrapes that happen every time clubs shift in the bag. They also happen to be one of the few places in golf where you can be completely unserious. Our Daphne's Headcovers range turns the top of your bag into a small zoo — black bears, black labs, armadillos, hedgehogs, llamas and hawks among them — and the Taboo sets bring coordinated prints if you would rather everything matched. Sweet Rollz grip wraps carry the same idea down the shaft, adding colour and a bit of extra cushioning where your hands sit.

Beyond the fun of it, there is a practical argument. A distinctive head cover makes your clubs instantly identifiable when four bags are loaded on a cart, and it is a small deterrent against a club walking off with someone else at the turn.

Belt bags, totes and the art of carrying less

Not every round calls for hauling a full bag between shots. A belt bag like the Daily Sports Hobart holds a phone, a couple of balls, tees and a ball marker, and keeps them on your hip where you can reach them without walking back to the cart. Crossbody and carry-all bags from Glove It work the same way off the course — they are sized for a range session, a lesson, or the drive to the club, and they coordinate with the larger bags in the same print if you like your kit to look deliberate.

Towels are the accessory people skip and then miss. A dedicated golf towel — ideally one with a clip and a waffle or microfibre face — keeps grooves clear so your wedges actually spin, and keeps your hands dry enough that the glove lasts longer. It is a small piece of kit that quietly improves ball striking.

Tees, markers and the small stuff

Martini Tees have a broader cup than a standard wooden tee, which makes them easier to set at a consistent height and less likely to snap on a heavy strike. They come in original and step-up versions, the latter giving you a fixed height for driver so your tee shots start from the same place every time. Consistency in setup is one of the cheapest improvements available in golf, and a tee that does not move is part of it.

Ball markers and hat clips are the accessory most likely to be borrowed and never returned, so it helps to have a spare. A marker that sits flat and does not catch the wind is more useful than a decorative one that blows across the green. Ball retrievers such as the Ball Rescue extend your reach into water and thick rough and pay for themselves over a season in balls recovered.

Cart seat covers and comfort on the course

Golf Chic quilted cart seat covers slip over the arm rests of most standard carts and give you a clean, cushioned surface in place of vinyl that has been baking in the sun. Standard covers measure 43 by 29 inches, with handle openings 40 inches apart. If you play a course with an older fleet, or you simply do not want to sit on someone else's afternoon, they are a straightforward upgrade — and they roll up small enough to live in your bag.

Sun Mountain push cart seats serve a similar purpose for walkers, turning a push cart into somewhere to rest between shots without carrying an extra chair.

How to build an accessory kit without overbuying

If you are starting from nothing, work in this order. First, sun protection: a visor or cap you like enough to wear every round. Second, a correctly fitted glove, ideally two. Third, a towel with a clip. Fourth, a supply of tees and at least two ball markers. Everything after that — head covers, belt bags, cart seat covers, grip wraps — is about comfort and personality rather than necessity, and it is the part that makes a golf bag feel like yours.

Accessories are also the easiest thing to buy for a golfer who already owns plenty of clothes. If you are shopping for someone else, a head cover, a set of tees and a marker together make a gift that gets used every single round, and our golf gifts for women and Tee Box subscription boxes bundle that thinking for you.

Questions about fit, sizing or what goes with what?

Accessories are personal, and photographs only tell you so much. If you are unsure whether a visor will suit your head shape, which glove size to order, or whether a bag will fit your clubs, get in touch through our contact page and we will help you work it out before you order. You can also browse the rest of the range in golf apparel, golf shoes and golf bags to build a look that hangs together from head to toe.

Women's Golf Bags: Choosing the One That Suits How You Play

A golf bag is the most personal piece of equipment you own that is not a club. It decides how much you carry, how organised you are, how your back feels at the end of eighteen holes, and — quietly — how put-together your whole set-up looks on the first tee. This collection covers the full range: cart bags and stand bags from Sun Mountain, coordinated carry-alls, shoe bags and totes from Glove It, belt bags from Daily Sports, and travel and lifestyle bags from Orca.

Start with one question: do you ride or walk?

Almost every other decision follows from this. If you ride a cart for most rounds, a cart bag is the right choice. Cart bags are built to sit securely on a cart with the pockets facing outward and accessible while the bag is strapped down, and because you are not carrying the weight, they can afford to be larger, better organised and more heavily padded. Sun Mountain's cart bags — the Boom 14-way, the Mid-Stripe 14-way and the Diva among them — give you a divider for every club, which prevents the shaft-on-shaft rattle that wears grips and paint.

If you walk, weight becomes the dominant concern, and a stand bag is what you want. Stand bags carry legs that deploy when you set the bag down, dual straps that spread load across both shoulders, and a deliberately lighter build. A Sunday bag such as the Sun Mountain SLx goes further still, stripping the bag back to a handful of clubs and the essentials for a quick nine or a range session.

If you do both, be honest about the split. A cart bag carried for one round will convince you never to walk again; a minimal stand bag on a cart leaves you fishing for pockets all day.

Dividers, pockets and what actually matters

Club dividers are counted as 4-way, 6-way, 14-way or full-length. More dividers means less club-on-club contact and easier retrieval, but also more weight and a slightly narrower opening for each club. A 14-way top is a genuine luxury on a cart bag. On a walking bag, 4- or 6-way with full-length dividers is usually the better compromise.

Pockets deserve more attention than they usually get. Look for a full-length apparel pocket big enough for a rain jacket and a pullover, an insulated pocket for water, a lined valuables pocket for a phone and keys, and at least one pocket you can reach while the bag is strapped to a cart. A rangefinder pocket with a magnetic closure is worth having if you use one, because it saves you zipping and unzipping on every approach.

Strap quality is the detail people regret ignoring. If you walk, a properly padded dual strap with an adjustable sternum connection transforms how a loaded bag feels after twelve holes. Single straps are lighter and fine for Sunday bags; for a full set, take the dual strap.

Belt bags and carrying less

There is a growing category of very small bags designed to hold only what you need between shots, and they solve a real problem. The Daily Sports Hobart belt bag holds a phone, a spare ball, tees and a marker on your hip, so you are not walking back to the cart every time you need something. If you play scramble formats, or you like to walk ahead to your ball while a partner drives, a belt bag is genuinely useful rather than merely fashionable.

The same thinking applies to crossbody and 2-zip carry-all bags from Glove It. They are sized for a lesson, a range hour, or the drive to the course, and they are far more pleasant than emptying a full golf bag into a handbag.

Shoe bags, towels and the supporting cast

A dedicated shoe bag keeps damp, grass-covered spikes away from clean clothes, and away from the interior of your car. Glove It's Augusta and Sea Glass shoe bags come in the same prints as their larger bags, so the whole set coordinates if that appeals to you. Pair one with a sport towel, a belt wristlet and a matching cap or visor and you have a complete, deliberate-looking kit without having thought about it very hard.

Orca's travel and lifestyle bags cover the other end of the spectrum — the duffel that goes on the golf trip, the piece that has to survive an airport rather than a fairway. If you travel to play, a proper travel cover for your clubs is not optional; airline handling is not kind to graphite shafts.

Weight, balance and your back

A fully loaded walking bag weighs a surprising amount once you add clubs, balls, water, a jacket and an umbrella. Two things reduce the strain more than any marketing feature. First, balanced weight distribution: the bag should hang close to your back rather than pulling away from it, which is what a well-designed dual strap and a good hip pad achieve. Second, ruthless editing — most golfers carry several items they never use. Emptying your bag completely at the start of each season and only putting back what you actually reached for last year is the single most effective weight reduction available.

If carrying is uncomfortable regardless, a push cart is the middle path between carrying and riding. Sun Mountain's Speed Cart V1R models fold compactly and take the entire load off your shoulders while still letting you walk the course, and our push cart collection includes seats and accessories to go with them.

Matching your bag to the rest of your kit

Golf bags last years, so it is worth choosing one you will still like. Coordinated ranges — Glove It's Augusta and Sea Glass collections, for example — let you match a bag, a cap, a visor, a towel and a shoe bag without guessing at colours. If you prefer a bag that disappears rather than announces itself, Sun Mountain's black, camo and neutral colourways go with everything and hide wear well.

A practical tip: if you buy a light-coloured bag, be realistic about maintenance. Bags pick up grass, mud and sunscreen. Wiping the base and the bottom of the pockets after a wet round keeps a pale bag looking new far longer than it otherwise would.

Care and storage

Empty the bag at the end of the season. Old balls, damp towels and half-eaten snacks are how a bag starts to smell. Wipe the interior, leave the pockets open to air, and store the bag upright somewhere dry rather than flat in a garage where moisture collects. Check zips occasionally; a little lubricant on a stiff zip prevents the forced tug that eventually breaks it.

Need help choosing?

Bag choice depends on details we cannot see from here — how far you walk, what you carry, whether your clubs are standard length. Tell us how you play through our contact page and we will point you to the right size and style. You can also browse golf accessories, golf shoes and golf apparel to finish the set.

Clearance: Women's Golf Clothes at Final-Sale Prices

This is where end-of-season styles, discontinued colourways and last-few-sizes pieces land. Everything here is genuinely reduced and genuinely limited — when a size sells out of a clearance line, it does not come back. If you are willing to be a little flexible about colour and quick about deciding, clearance is the most efficient way to build a golf wardrobe.

What ends up on this page, and why

Clearance stock is not lesser stock. Pieces arrive here for four ordinary reasons. Sometimes a brand discontinues a print or colour and moves on to the next season's palette, leaving perfectly good garments without a home. Sometimes we are down to two or three sizes in a style and it no longer makes sense to keep it in the main collection. Sometimes a seasonal item — a lined pullover, a lightweight summer skort — reaches the wrong end of the calendar. And sometimes we simply bought more of something than we sold.

What you will currently find spans Puma golf dresses, skirts and shorts, Kinona tops, skorts and pants, Tail Activewear golf and tennis pieces, EP Pro NY polos and skorts, GGBlue shorts and shirts, Belyn Key tops, Smith & Quinn skirts, Duca Del Cosma shoes and more. The mix changes constantly, which is the best argument for checking back.

How to shop clearance well

The golfers who do best on this page follow a few habits. The first is knowing their measurements rather than their nominal size. Golf brands size differently from one another, and clearance is exactly the situation where you cannot afford to guess — there is rarely a second chance at the same piece in a different size. Our size charts list brand-specific measurements; take five minutes with a tape measure once and you will buy more confidently forever.

The second habit is shopping for gaps rather than for bargains. A reduced price on something you will not wear is not a saving. Before browsing, make a short mental list of what your wardrobe is actually missing — a mid-layer, a pair of pants that works in cold weather, a sleeveless top for high summer — and filter by that.

The third is buying out of season deliberately. Outerwear is cheapest in spring, sleeveless tops are cheapest in autumn, and neither goes out of date in the intervening months. If you are building a wardrobe rather than filling an urgent gap, buying one season ahead is the single biggest lever you have.

Understanding "final sale"

Many clearance items are marked final sale, and that designation matters. Please read the terms on our shipping and returns page before ordering, and note the general policy: new, unworn items may be returned within 30 days of delivery for a refund minus return shipping, with returns initiated after 30 days resulting in store credit. Items specifically marked final sale fall outside that, so choose carefully.

This is not a reason to avoid clearance — it is a reason to do the measuring first. If you are between sizes and cannot decide, or you are unsure how a particular brand runs, ask us before you order rather than after. We would far rather spend two minutes checking a garment measurement than have you end up with something that does not fit.

Fit notes worth knowing before you order

A few patterns hold across most golf brands and are useful when you cannot try something on. Skorts and skirts are usually listed by the length of the skirt portion, measured from the waist — a 16-inch skort sits noticeably shorter than an 18-inch. If you have a preferred length in something you already own, measure it and shop to that number rather than to a description.

Polos and sleeveless tops vary most in the shoulder and the armhole. If you have found a brand that fits your shoulders well, that brand will usually keep fitting you across styles, which makes brand-loyal clearance shopping lower risk than jumping between makers.

Pants and shorts are listed by inseam as well as size. Golf pants in particular are cut long by design, because they are meant to sit over a shoe rather than above it. If you are petite, check the inseam before the waist size — our petite collection exists because the standard inseam is the usual problem.

Making clearance pieces work together

The risk with discounted shopping is ending up with a wardrobe of orphans — individually appealing pieces that do not combine. The fix is to anchor on neutrals. If your bottoms are navy, black, white or a muted tone, almost any top on this page will work with them. Buy the bold prints as tops and the quiet colours as bottoms, and a handful of clearance purchases will produce far more outfits than the same number bought the other way round.

Outer layers are the other reliable clearance buy. A vest or a wind layer in a neutral colour goes over everything, is rarely tied to a season's trend, and is the piece most likely to still be in your bag in five years.

New stock arrives regularly

Because clearance is driven by what is selling and what the brands are discontinuing, this page turns over continuously rather than on a schedule. Sizes come and go within days on popular styles. If you see something in your size that fills a real gap, it is worth acting rather than waiting for a further reduction that may never come — most clearance pieces sell out before they are marked down again.

You can also keep an eye on our sales collection for reductions on current-season stock, and subscribe to our email list for member-only promotions.

Questions about a specific piece?

If you want a garment measurement, a fabric composition, or an honest opinion on how a particular style runs before you commit to a final-sale purchase, get in touch through our contact page. We would rather help you get it right the first time. You can also browse the full golf apparel, bottoms and tops collections at regular prices.

The Fore Ladies Tee Box: A Women's Golf Subscription Box, Explained

We built the Tee Box around a simple observation: golfers rarely treat themselves. We replace a glove when it falls apart, buy a new top when the old one fades, and otherwise get on with it. A subscription box breaks that pattern, because something arrives whether or not you got around to shopping — and because someone else has done the choosing, you end up with things you would never have picked but genuinely like.

The Fore Ladies Tee Box is a monthly women's golf subscription box of carefully selected items that celebrate you. It is also, in our experience, one of the most reliably well-received golf gifts for women, because it arrives twelve times instead of once.

What arrives in a Tee Box

Each month brings a surprise loaded with name-brand golf apparel, golf accessories, fair trade teas, protein and energy bars, and other golf-related items from small independent companies — companies like ours. Across the year you can expect a combination of name-brand golf apparel, golf-themed graphic tees, name-brand golf balls, the latest in golf gear and accessories, and custom-made health and beauty items chosen from independent, woman-owned businesses.

No two boxes are the same. That is the point of it: the pleasure of a subscription box is the opening, and a predictable box is just a slower way of shopping.

Tee Box "Light" for accessories only

Some golfers love the idea of a subscription but have no need for more apparel — the wardrobe is full, the sizing is particular, or the clothes simply are not the interesting part. The Tee Box "Light" answers that. Each month it contains the same fun accessories as the full Tee Box, without the clothing.

A Light box will include items such as golf balls, golf towels, zip bags, shoe bags, golf tees, ball markers, practice tools, and the same carefully chosen health and beauty items from independent, woman-owned businesses. If you are buying for someone whose size you do not know, Light removes the only real risk in gifting a subscription.

Choosing your subscription length

The standard Tee Box is a one-month renewing subscription that renews automatically for the period you choose. We also offer three-month and six-month subscriptions, and the choice between them is really a choice about who the box is for.

If you are subscribing for yourself, the rolling monthly option is the most flexible. If you are buying it as a gift, a defined three- or six-month run is usually the better choice — the recipient gets a clear, generous present with a known end point, and there is no awkwardness about who is paying for month seven.

Six months covers most of a playing season in a temperate climate, which makes it a strong choice for a birthday early in the year. Three months works well as a Christmas gift that carries someone through the off-season and into spring.

Buying a Tee Box as a gift

Two practical details make the difference between a gift that lands and one that goes astray. First, when you order a Tee Box subscription as a gift, enter your recipient's address as the shipping address at checkout rather than your own. Second, remember that the subscription renews automatically after the period you choose, so decide in advance whether you intend it to continue.

If you are looking for our Birdie gift box rather than the subscription, it lives on our gift box page alongside the one-time Surprise Boxes.

When boxes ship

Tee Boxes ship during the first week of every month. Boxes purchased after the fifteenth of the month will ship as part of the following month's subscription, so if you are buying for a specific date it is worth ordering early in the month rather than late. Tracking is sent as soon as it is available. Full details are on our shipping and returns page, including the Tee Box policy: boxes are final sale and are not eligible for return, though size exchanges for Tee Box apparel can be requested through the exchange form linked there.

Why a subscription rather than a one-off gift

There is a reason subscription boxes have held their popularity in golf specifically. Golf equipment and apparel are both areas where the good stuff is easy to miss — small brands do not get shelf space, and the big retailers stock what sells in volume. A curated box is a filter. Somebody who spends their working life looking at women's golf products decides what goes in, which means you see things you would not have found by searching.

The second reason is pacing. A single large gift is enjoyed once. A subscription creates a small event every month, usually at exactly the point in the season when motivation dips. Plenty of our subscribers describe the box arriving as the thing that got them back out to the range in February.

The third is discovery of the independent brands themselves. A significant share of what we include comes from small, often woman-owned companies making one thing very well. Those are the items that tend to get bought again directly once someone has tried them.

A note on value and how we choose

The items in each box are chosen for how often they will be used rather than to hit a number on a spreadsheet. That means a box may contain one substantial piece of apparel and several smaller items, or no apparel at all and a broader spread of accessories and treats — it depends on what is genuinely good that month. We would rather send something you will reach for every round than pad a box to look fuller.

The independent and woman-owned brands we include are a deliberate part of that. They are the makers who do not get shelf space at large retailers, and they are consistently the items subscribers write to us about.

Tennis players welcome

If the person you are buying for plays tennis rather than golf — or both — the Grand Slam Box applies the same curation to tennis apparel and accessories. You will find it alongside our tennis apparel collection.

Questions before you subscribe?

If you want to know more about how sizing is handled, how to pause or manage a subscription, or what has appeared in recent boxes, get in touch through our contact page and we will answer honestly. You can also browse all subscription and gift boxes, golf gifts for women and golf accessories while you decide.

Women's Golf Gift Boxes: A Present She Will Actually Use

Buying for a golfer is harder than it looks. She already owns clubs. You do not know her size, and guessing wrong turns a gift into an errand. Gift cards work, but they do not feel like much when they are opened. Our women's golf gift boxes exist to solve exactly that problem: a curated selection of accessories, treats and course-day essentials, packed together, sent with a personal card, and chosen so that everything inside gets used rather than shelved.

What a Fore Ladies gift box actually is

Each box is a one-time purchase, not a subscription. You choose a box, we pack it, and it arrives ready to give. No two Surprise Boxes are identical, which is part of the appeal — the recipient is opening something genuinely unexpected rather than a product she could have priced on a shelf. Every box ships with a card carrying your personal message, which you add in the Notes section at checkout.

The boxes are built around accessories rather than apparel, which is deliberate. Accessories sidestep the sizing problem entirely. A golf towel, a set of tees, a divot tool or a crossbody bag works regardless of what size she wears, and these are the things golfers use every single round without ever quite getting around to buying for themselves.

Choosing between the boxes

We build the Surprise Boxes at several levels so you can match the gift to the occasion rather than the other way round.

Fun & Games is the lightest of the group, with a combined retail value of at least $95. It contains a dozen practice balls, a coordinating hat, coordinating golf socks, a coordinating drinks tumbler, a coordinating Glove It crossbody bag, and a card game to play during a round. The coordination is the point here — the pieces are chosen to go together, so it reads as a considered set rather than a handful of items.

Albatross steps up to a combined retail value of at least $170 and broadens the range considerably. Expect a combination of golf balls, a golf belt, golf socks, a golf book, sunscreen, Martini tees, a hat or visor, a crossbody bag, a divot repair tool, club and shoe cleaners, ball marker alligator clips, a golf rules card set, a golf towel with a zipper pocket, self-care serums and sprays from Orglamix, a Puma soft-sided drinks and snacks cooler, and a card game.

Hole-In-One is the most generous of the Surprise Boxes, with a combined retail value of at least $220 drawn from the same carefully chosen range. It is the box to pick for a milestone — a significant birthday, a retirement, a first club championship, or the friend who has quietly done something worth marking.

Eagle boxes are also available, and our subscription and gift box collection shows the full current line-up alongside three-month and six-month options if you would rather the gift kept arriving.

If the recipient has a clear preference between a hat and a visor, add that note at checkout and we will pack accordingly.

Matching the box to the occasion

Different occasions call for different weights of gift, and it helps to think about it that way rather than purely by price.

For a golf-trip send-off or a league secret-santa, Fun & Games hits the right note: playful, useful, and clearly chosen for a golfer rather than pulled off a general gift shelf. The card game in particular tends to get used on the trip itself, which is a nice touch.

For a birthday, Mother's Day or a thank-you, Albatross is the natural middle. There is enough variety that something will be a genuine surprise, and the mix of on-course items and self-care products means it works whether she plays weekly or occasionally.

For Christmas, a big anniversary, or a group gift from several people, Hole-In-One carries the weight the occasion needs without you having to assemble anything yourself.

For a tennis player rather than a golfer, we also build the Grand Slam Box along the same principles.

Why boxes beat single items as gifts

There is a practical reason a curated box lands better than one nice thing. Golfers accumulate single accessories slowly and inconsistently — a glove here, a towel two years later — so the contents of most bags are a mismatched archive rather than a set. A box replaces several tired items at once and brings them into line with each other. The effect on opening day is that a bag suddenly looks and feels new without a single club changing.

There is also the discovery element. Most of us buy the same brands repeatedly because we know them. A curated box introduces small independent makers, woman-owned brands and products a shopper would not have searched for, and it is common for one of those to become the item she then buys again on her own.

Practical notes before you order

If you are shipping the gift directly to the recipient, enter her address as the shipping address at checkout rather than your own. Add your gift message in the Notes field at the same time — this is what gets printed on the card that travels with the box.

Gift boxes are final sale and are not eligible for return, so it is worth reading the full terms on our shipping and returns page before ordering. Size exchanges for apparel included in a box can be requested through the exchange form linked there.

Timing matters around holidays. If the box needs to arrive by a particular date, order with room to spare rather than at the last moment, and get in touch if you are working to a tight deadline so we can tell you honestly whether it will make it.

Still deciding?

If you know a little about the person you are buying for — how often she plays, whether she walks or rides, whether she is more likely to appreciate on-course gear or something for afterwards — we can help you choose between the boxes. Get in touch through our contact page.

And if a box is not quite right, our golf gifts for women guide covers individual gift ideas by budget and occasion, while the Fore Ladies Tee Box turns a single gift into a monthly one. You can also browse accessories and golf apparel to build something yourself.

Golf Gifts for Women: How to Choose Something She Will Actually Use

On the hunt for the perfect golf gift for a woman who plays? You are in the right place — and you have arrived with a harder brief than you probably realise. Golf is a sport where the obvious gifts are either too personal to guess at (clubs, shoes, anything with a size on the label) or so generic they feel like an afterthought. This guide is our attempt to make the decision straightforward, organised by what you know about her and how much you want to spend.

Start with what you know

Before browsing, answer three questions. Does she play regularly or occasionally? Does she walk or ride? And is she the kind of golfer who enjoys the gear, the fashion, or mainly the game itself? Those three answers narrow the field faster than any price filter.

A regular player has most of the basics but wears them out — gloves, towels, tees and markers are consumables for her, and a fresh supply is genuinely welcome. An occasional player is more likely to be missing whole categories, so a head cover, a belt bag or a decent towel fills a real gap. Someone who walks values weight and organisation; someone who rides values cart comfort. A golfer who enjoys the fashion side will appreciate something in a print; a player focused on the game will appreciate something that solves a problem.

Gifts under a modest budget

Small gifts work when they are things she will use every round and would not think to replace. Martini Tees are a good example — a broader cup makes them easier to set at a consistent height and harder to snap, and the step-up version gives a repeatable driver height. A pair of ball markers and a hat clip solve the most-frequently-lost-item problem. A golf towel with a clip is the item golfers most often make do without and most appreciate receiving.

Daphne's head covers sit in this bracket too, and they are one of the most reliably well-received gifts we sell. A black bear, a black lab, an armadillo, a hedgehog or a llama on the top of a bag is both practical protection and a small daily pleasure. Sweet Rollz grip wraps do something similar further down the club.

Mid-range gifts that feel considered

This is where accessories become meaningful. A Glove It crossbody or 2-zip carry-all bag, a coordinating visor or cap, a belt wristlet, or a Daily Sports Hobart belt bag all land well because they are things a golfer notices other people having and rarely buys for herself. A Golf Chic quilted cart seat cover is a strong choice for anyone who rides — it slips over the arm rests of most standard carts and replaces sun-baked vinyl with something clean and cushioned.

Sun protection also sits here, and it is a more thoughtful gift than it sounds. A UV-protective shoulder wrap or cooling sleeve means she is not reapplying sunscreen every few holes, and a wide-brim straw hat such as the Daily Sports Dubbo covers neck and ears as well as face.

If you want the decision made for you, our curated golf gift boxes start at this level. The Fun & Games box carries a combined retail value of at least $95 and contains practice balls, a coordinating hat, socks, a drinks tumbler, a Glove It crossbody bag and a card game for the round.

Generous gifts for milestones

For a significant birthday, a retirement, or a first club championship, the two strongest options are a curated box at the larger end or a genuine piece of equipment. Our Albatross box carries a combined retail value of at least $170 and Hole-In-One at least $220, each drawing from golf balls, belts, socks, books, sunscreen, Martini tees, a hat or visor, crossbody bags, divot tools, club and shoe cleaners, ball marker clips, a rules card set, a towel with a zipper pocket, Orglamix self-care products, a Puma soft-sided cooler and a card game.

Alternatively, a bag is a gift that lasts years. Sun Mountain cart and stand bags, Glove It coordinated sets and Orca travel bags are all in our golf bags collection, and a push cart from the push cart range is transformative for anyone who walks and has started to find it a strain.

The gift that keeps arriving

If you want the gift to be remembered past the day it is opened, a Fore Ladies Tee Box subscription delivers a curated surprise every month — name-brand golf apparel, accessories, fair trade teas, protein and energy bars, and products from small independent companies. There is also a Tee Box "Light" for someone who would rather receive accessories than clothing, and three-month and six-month options if you prefer a defined run rather than a rolling subscription.

For tennis players, the Grand Slam Box follows the same idea.

Gifts to approach with caution

Three categories cause more returns than they are worth unless you are very confident. Apparel is the obvious one — sizing varies significantly between golf brands, and our size charts exist precisely because a size 8 in one brand is not a size 8 in another. Shoes are worse, because width matters as much as length. And gloves need to fit snugly across the palm to work at all.

If your heart is set on apparel, a safe approach is to choose something forgiving — a vest, an outer layer or an accessory-adjacent piece — rather than a fitted polo or skort. Or simply ask. Most golfers will happily tell you their size if the alternative is a gift that does not fit.

A note on presentation

Golf gifts benefit disproportionately from arriving well. Our gift boxes ship with a card carrying your personal message, added in the Notes section at checkout, and if you are sending directly to the recipient, enter her address as the shipping address rather than your own. Gift boxes are final sale, so please read the terms on our shipping and returns page before ordering.

Need a second opinion?

If you are stuck between two options, or you know almost nothing about her golf habits and would rather not ask, tell us what you do know through our contact page and we will help you narrow it down. You can also browse accessories, golf apparel and clearance for ideas across every budget.

/outerwear.desc_html:
Women's Golf Outerwear: Layers That Let You Keep Playing

Golf does not wait for perfect weather. Some of the best rounds of the year are the ones played in a breeze off the water, on a damp autumn morning, or on a spring day that starts cold and finishes warm. Outerwear is what makes those rounds enjoyable instead of merely survivable — and, crucially, it is what lets you keep making a full swing when the temperature drops. This collection brings together the wind jackets, midlayers, softshells, vests and knitwear that handle the weather without turning you into a marshmallow at address.

The rule that governs all golf outerwear: it has to let you swing

Ordinary outdoor jackets are designed for standing, walking and sitting. A golf jacket has to survive a full shoulder turn, repeated a hundred times, without riding up, binding across the back, or rustling at the top of the backswing. That is why the pieces here are cut with articulated sleeves, stretch through the shoulders and back, and hems that stay put. It is also why so many golf jackets are short-sleeved or sleeveless — removing fabric from the arms removes the most common source of restriction.

When you are trying outerwear on, do not judge it standing still in front of a mirror. Make a slow practice swing. Reach across your body. If the fabric pulls at the shoulder blades or the cuff drags down the back of your hand, it is the wrong piece, however good it looks.

Wind jackets: the most-used piece in most bags

If you only own one piece of golf outerwear, make it a wind jacket. Wind is far more common than rain on a golf course, and it strips away warmth faster than low temperature alone. A good wind layer is thin enough to pack into a bag pocket, blocks the breeze across the chest and shoulders, and breathes enough that you are not damp from the inside by the ninth.

The Daily Sports Angelet range is a useful illustration of how one idea gets cut three ways. The full wind jacket gives you complete coverage for cold, exposed courses. The short-sleeve version keeps your core warm while leaving the arms entirely free — a favourite of players who find long sleeves distracting. The wind vest strips it back further, protecting the torso only, which is often exactly enough on a mild but blustery day. Owning two of the three is not excessive; they cover genuinely different conditions.

Midlayers and softshells for real cold

When the temperature drops properly, a single shell is not enough, and the answer is layering rather than one thick coat. A midlayer — the Daily Sports Cholet full-zip or the Bayonne midlayer jacket, for example — sits between your polo and your outer shell, holding warm air without bulk. A full zip lets you dump heat quickly on an uphill walk and close it again on an exposed tee.

Softshell hybrids such as the Abacus Dornoch and Navan jackets take a different approach: they combine a wind- and weather-resistant front panel with a stretch knit back and sleeves. The result is a single garment that behaves like two — protected where the weather hits you, mobile where you need to move. For many golfers this is the sweet spot for autumn and early spring, and it is the piece that ends up living in the boot of the car all season.

Vests: warmth where you need it, freedom where you do not

Vests are the most under-appreciated category in golf outerwear. Keeping your core warm is what keeps your muscles loose; keeping your arms unencumbered is what keeps your swing long. A vest does both at once. Quilted and lightly padded styles like the Daily Sports Caen add genuine insulation for cold mornings. Knit vests such as the Scratch Seventy V-neck and the Sun Mountain Colter work as a smart midlayer that looks entirely at home in a clubhouse afterwards. Golftini City Girl vests lean further towards style, which matters when the round ends at lunch.

A practical note: if you are between two pieces and cannot decide, the vest is almost always the one you will reach for more often across a full season.

Knitwear and pullovers for the shoulder seasons

There is a stretch of the calendar — roughly the first and last few weeks of the season — where a jacket is too much and a polo alone is too little. That is pullover weather. Cable-knit sweaters and roll-neck pullovers from Daily Sports handle it with real fabric rather than technical shells, and they have the advantage of looking good off the course as well as on it. Lined versions add warmth for early tee times; unlined versions are better once the sun is up.

V-neck and half-neck styles matter more than they appear to. A V-neck leaves your collar visible, which reads as traditional golf and works with almost any polo underneath. A roll or half-neck gives you extra warmth at the throat, which is where a lot of people feel the cold first. Both are worth having if you play through a proper winter.

Fabric, care and making outerwear last

Technical outerwear underperforms when it is dirty. Body oils and sunscreen clog the fabric and reduce breathability, so a wind jacket that feels clammy after two seasons usually just needs washing properly rather than replacing. Follow the care label, wash on a gentle cycle, skip the fabric softener — it coats the fibres and kills wicking — and avoid high heat in the dryer, which can damage laminates and elastic.

Knitwear asks for the opposite kind of care. Store sweaters folded rather than hung, so the shoulders do not stretch, and give cable knits a rest day between wears to let the fibres recover their shape. Both types benefit from being fully dry before they go back in the bag; a damp jacket stuffed into a pocket is how mildew starts.

Building a layering system that works

Think in three layers and you will rarely be caught out. Next to the skin, a moisture-wicking polo or long-sleeve top from our tops collection moves sweat away. In the middle, a knit pullover or midlayer holds warm air. On the outside, a wind or softshell jacket blocks weather. On a cold, still day you might use layers one and two. On a mild, windy day, layers one and three. On a genuinely raw morning, all three — and you shed them as the round warms up.

Sizing across layers is worth a moment of thought. Buy your base layer to fit close, your midlayer to fit comfortably over it, and your shell with just enough room that nothing compresses. If you size everything identically, the outer layer will bind exactly where you need movement.

Not sure what your climate needs?

Outerwear is the category where local conditions matter most — a jacket that is perfect for a cold Midwest October is far too much for a mild desert winter. If you tell us where and when you play, we will help you work out which pieces earn their place in your bag. Reach out through our contact page, check brand-specific measurements on our size charts, and browse bottoms and golf apparel to complete the look.

Golf Subscription Boxes and Gift Boxes for Women

Everything we curate into a box lives on this page — the rolling Tee Box subscriptions, the fixed three- and six-month runs, the accessories-only Tee Box "Light", the one-time Surprise Gift Boxes, and the Grand Slam Box for tennis players. If you are choosing between them, the short version is this: subscriptions are for ongoing delight, gift boxes are for a single occasion, and both remove the sizing risk that makes buying for a golfer difficult.

Subscriptions: the gift that keeps arriving

The Fore Ladies Tee Box is a monthly women's golf subscription box of carefully selected items. Each month brings a surprise loaded with name-brand golf apparel, golf accessories, fair trade teas, protein and energy bars, and other golf-related items from small independent companies. Across a subscription you can expect name-brand apparel, golf-themed graphic tees, name-brand golf balls, current gear and accessories, and custom-made health and beauty items from independent, woman-owned businesses.

Subscriptions come in three forms. The standard monthly option renews automatically for the period you choose and suits someone subscribing for themselves. The three-month subscription works well as a defined gift — generous, clear, with a known end point. The six-month subscription covers most of a playing season, which makes it a strong choice for a birthday early in the year.

Tee Boxes ship during the first week of every month, and boxes purchased after the fifteenth ship with the following month's subscription. There is more detail on how it all works on the Tee Box page.

Tee Box "Light" for accessories only

If the recipient has plenty of clothes, or you simply do not know her size, the Tee Box "Light" delivers the same fun accessories as the full box without the apparel — golf balls, towels, zip bags, shoe bags, tees, ball markers, practice tools, and the same health and beauty items from independent makers. It is the lowest-risk subscription to give as a gift.

One-time Surprise Gift Boxes

If you want a single, complete present rather than a recurring one, the Surprise Gift Boxes are packed and ready to give, each shipping with a card carrying your personal message.

The Fun & Games box has a combined retail value of at least $95 and contains a dozen practice balls, a coordinating hat, coordinating golf socks, a coordinating drinks tumbler, a coordinating Glove It crossbody bag and a card game for the round. Albatross steps up to a combined retail value of at least $170, and Hole-In-One to at least $220, both drawing from a wider range that can include golf balls, belts, socks, books, sunscreen, Martini tees, a hat or visor, crossbody bags, a divot repair tool, club and shoe cleaners, ball marker alligator clips, a golf rules card set, a golf towel with a zipper pocket, Orglamix self-care products, a Puma soft-sided cooler and a card game. Eagle boxes are available alongside them.

No two Surprise Boxes are identical, which is deliberate — the pleasure is in the opening. Full contents and current availability are on the gift box page.

Which one should you choose?

Pick a one-time gift box when there is a specific occasion and you want something substantial to hand over on the day. Pick a three- or six-month subscription when you want the gift to keep being noticed, or when the occasion is significant enough to warrant it. Pick Tee Box Light when you do not know her size and would rather not ask. Pick the rolling monthly subscription when you are treating yourself.

For a tennis player, the Grand Slam Box applies the same curation to tennis apparel and accessories, and pairs naturally with our tennis apparel collection.

Ordering as a gift

Two details matter. Enter the recipient's address as the shipping address at checkout rather than your own, and add your gift message in the Notes field so it can be printed on the card that travels with the box. If she has a clear preference between a hat and a visor, note that too.

Boxes and subscriptions are final sale and are not eligible for return. Size exchanges for Tee Box apparel can be requested through the form linked on our shipping and returns page, which also covers shipping timing in full.

Why curated boxes work for golfers specifically

Golf is a category where the interesting products are easy to miss. Small brands rarely get shelf space, and large retailers stock what sells in volume, so most golfers cycle through the same handful of names. A curated box is a filter run by someone who spends their working life looking at women's golf products, which is how you end up with things you would never have searched for and then use constantly.

There is also the matter of pacing. One large gift is enjoyed once. A box arriving each month creates a small event, often at exactly the point in the season when enthusiasm dips and a nudge back to the range is welcome.

What happens after the first box

A recurring question is what a subscription looks like month two onwards, and the honest answer is that variety is the whole design. Because the contents change each month and are drawn from different brands, the boxes do not repeat — a month heavy on apparel may be followed by one built around accessories and treats. Over a six-month run you end up with a genuinely broad cross-section of what is current in women's golf rather than six versions of the same idea.

That variety is also why subscriptions suit golfers at different stages. A newer player fills gaps she did not know she had. Building a tennis wardrobe that actually works

Tennis asks different things of clothing than golf does. Where golf is a long, steady walk punctuated by rotation, tennis is short bursts of sprinting, lunging and overhead reaching, repeated for an hour or more. Clothing has to move in every direction, stay put through sudden changes of pace, and handle far more sweat in far less time. That is why tennis pieces are cut closer, built lighter, and almost always paired with built-in shorties or a bra.

A practical wardrobe is smaller than most people expect. Two or three skirts, three or four tops, one dress, one warm layer and a pair of shorties will cover a season of regular play. The thing to prioritise is not variety but drying time — if you play twice a week, you need pieces that are dry and ready again quickly.

Tennis skirts: length, pleats and pockets

Skirt length is the first decision and the most personal. Shorter skirts in the 12-inch range, like the Lucky In Love scallop and ombre star styles, give maximum freedom and are the traditional choice for competitive play. Longer 13.5-inch and 14-inch cuts — the pleated Tahiti and Chroma styles, the Amour flounce — offer more coverage without meaningfully restricting movement, and they are increasingly what players choose for club and social tennis.

Pleats are not purely decorative. A pleated skirt opens as you move and closes as you stop, which gives you a wider range of motion than a straight-cut skirt of the same length. Flounce and scallop hems do something similar with a softer line.

Pockets deserve attention if you serve. A skirt with a ball pocket — either a built-in short with a pocket or a side pocket in the skirt itself — means you are not holding a second ball in your non-dominant hand through a service motion. It is a small thing that makes practice sessions considerably easier.

Tops, tanks and built-in support

Tennis tops divide roughly into tanks, camis and long-sleeve crews, and the choice is mostly about sun, temperature and how much support you want built in. Lucky In Love's ribbed Henley tanks, Wave Runner camis, breezy bralette camis and V-neck tanks with built-in bras cover the range from light coverage to genuine support, and the built-in-bra styles remove a layer, which in hot weather is worth more than it sounds.

Long-sleeve crews and hi-lo tops have earned a permanent place in tennis wardrobes for sun protection rather than warmth. A lightweight long sleeve in a breathable knit is often cooler in direct sun than bare arms and sunscreen, and it removes the reapplication problem entirely during a long match.

Tennis dresses: one decision instead of two

The tennis dress endures because it solves the coordination problem in a single garment. There is no matching to think about, no top riding up over a skirt waistband, and modern dresses are built with an integrated short or bra so nothing needs layering underneath. TAIL Activewear and ella belle both cut dresses that work as hard on court as they look off it, which matters if your match is followed by lunch.

If you are buying one dress, choose a mid-length with a built-in short and a colour you can wear repeatedly. If you are buying a second, that is the moment for the print.

Fabric, colour and caring for tennis kit

Tennis clothing lives or dies on its recovery — how well it returns to shape after being stretched hard and washed often. Treat it like technical kit rather than casual clothing: cool wash, no fabric softener, and air drying rather than a hot dryer, which degrades elastane faster than anything else. Wash promptly rather than leaving damp kit in a bag, where sweat breaks down fibres and sets odour.

On colour: white remains required at some clubs, so it is worth owning at least one white skirt and top even if you prefer colour. Beyond that, bright colours and prints are part of why tennis clothing is fun, and our brands lean into it — Lucky In Love's Shocking Pink, C'est La Vie and Tahiti prints, TAIL's seasonal palettes, and ella belle's camo and floral patterns among them.

Shorties, layers and the supporting pieces

Shorties worn under a skirt or dress are not optional for most players — they prevent chafing, hold a ball, and let you move without thinking about coverage. Our shorties collection covers the options, and many players buy a pair in black and a pair in white to cover both wardrobes.

For cool mornings and indoor courts, a light jacket or long-sleeve layer that comes off easily matters more than a warm one. You will be warm within ten minutes of starting, so the priority is something you can remove without interrupting play.

Tennis racket bags and crossbody bags from Glove It round out the kit, and you will find them alongside our bags collection.

Women's Golf Shoes: Where Comfort, Traction and Style Meet

A round of golf is a long walk with roughly seventy full-body rotations built into it. No other piece of equipment works as hard as your shoes, and none has as direct an effect on both comfort and ball striking. Get them right and you stop thinking about your feet entirely. Get them wrong and you are managing a blister from the sixth hole onwards. This collection brings together women's golf shoes from Duca Del Cosma, Daily Sports, Aerogreen and Pakira — brands chosen because they take women's lasts and women's foot shapes seriously rather than shrinking a men's design.

Spiked or spikeless: which one is for you?

This is the first decision, and there is no universally correct answer. Spiked shoes use replaceable soft cleats that bite into turf. They give you the most traction on wet grass, on slopes and in the rough, and they are the safer choice if you play a hilly course or a links in the wind. The trade-off is that they are less comfortable on hard surfaces — cart paths, clubhouse floors, the car park — and the cleats need replacing periodically.

Spikeless shoes use a moulded outsole with lugs or dimples instead of removable cleats. They are lighter, they feel more like a trainer, and you can wear them from the car to the first tee to lunch without changing. On dry, flat courses they provide plenty of grip. On a wet, steep day they will eventually let go. Many golfers end up owning one of each and choosing by the forecast.

If you are buying your first pair and you mostly play in fair weather, spikeless is the easier, more versatile choice. If you play year-round in a climate with real rain, start with spiked.

Waterproofing is not optional in most climates

Wet feet ruin rounds faster than almost anything else, and morning dew soaks shoes just as thoroughly as rain does. Waterproof uppers — whether full-grain leather or a treated synthetic — keep that out. Pay attention to whether a shoe is described as genuinely waterproof or merely water-resistant, and to the length of any warranty the brand offers, because that warranty is usually the clearest signal of how confident the maker is.

Waterproofing does come at a small cost in breathability. If you play mainly in dry heat, a more breathable, lightly treated shoe will be more comfortable than a fully sealed one. This is another case where the honest answer depends on where you play rather than on which shoe is objectively better.

Fit: the part most people get wrong

Feet swell over the course of a round, which is why golf shoes are best fitted in the afternoon rather than first thing in the morning, and why they should have a little more room than your everyday shoes. Aim for roughly a thumb's width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Your heel should not lift when you walk. The shoe should hold your midfoot firmly — that is what stops your foot sliding during the downswing — without pinching across the widest part.

Width matters as much as length and is far more often ignored. If you have tried several golf shoes and they all felt tight across the ball of the foot, the issue is almost certainly width rather than size, and going up a full size to compensate will simply give you a shoe that is too long. Look for brands that offer genuine width options, and check the size charts, since golf shoe sizing varies noticeably between European and American brands.

Fit the shoe with the socks you will actually play in. A cushioned golf sock can take up a surprising amount of room, and a shoe fitted with a thin liner will feel completely different on the course.

How shoes affect your swing

Your swing starts from the ground. The sequence that produces clubhead speed begins with pressure shifting through your feet, and anything that lets your foot slide inside the shoe leaks energy out of that sequence. A shoe that locks your heel and midfoot in place gives you something to push against. This is why golf shoes are built with more lateral support than running shoes — running is a straight-line activity, and golf very much is not.

Stability does not have to mean stiffness. Current women's golf shoes, including the Duca Del Cosma range, use lightweight materials and cushioned midsoles that absorb the impact of several miles of walking while still holding the foot. If you have previously found golf shoes clumpy compared to trainers, it is worth trying a recent pair; the category has changed considerably.

Style that works beyond the course

There is no longer any reason for golf shoes to look like golf shoes. Duca Del Cosma's Festiva, Queenscup, Caldes, Kubana, Boreal, Bellezza and Alexa styles span everything from clean white leather to navy, silver, red, light blue and printed finishes. Many pass comfortably as smart trainers, which matters if your round is followed by lunch or you are travelling to a course and would rather not pack two pairs.

Colour choice is practical as well as aesthetic. White and light shoes show grass stains and mud quickly but look crisp with almost any outfit. Navy, black and darker patterns hide wear and suit a wider range of conditions. If this is your only pair, a mid-tone or patterned shoe will look good for longer.

Caring for golf shoes so they last

Brush grass and soil off the outsole after every round, while it is still damp and comes away easily. Wipe the upper with a cloth. If the shoes are genuinely wet, let them dry slowly at room temperature with the insoles removed — never on a radiator or in direct sun, which cracks leather and can unglue soles. Shoe trees or loosely crumpled paper help them hold their shape while drying.

If you play in spiked shoes, check the cleats every few rounds. Worn cleats are a slip hazard and they wear unevenly, which subtly changes how you stand. Replacing them is inexpensive and takes minutes. Rotating between two pairs, if you have them, roughly doubles the life of both by letting each dry out fully.

Choosing your next pair

Start with where you play and in what weather, then narrow by spiked or spikeless, then by width, then by style. If you are between two sizes, it is worth trying both and keeping the one that fits — trying to make a nearly-right shoe work over a full season rarely ends well. Our returns policy covers new, unworn items, so you can make that decision properly at home on carpet.
